migrationNotes: Spine: follow one stone. Drop it and say how fast it goes, then how far it falls, then throw it up and watch gravity at the top, and last ask whether a heavy stone falls faster.

lesson.title: Falling and rising

steps.headline: A stone speeds up as it falls

lead.text: Let go of a stone and gravity pulls it towards the ground. Film it and measure its velocity, and you find that it picks up the same amount every second: 10 m/s after one second, 30 m/s after three. A steady gain every second is a constant acceleration, as in the last lesson, so gravity gives the stone one.

That acceleration has its own letter, g. Near the Earth's surface it is 9.8 m/s², and this course uses 10 m/s² to keep the sums short unless a question says otherwise. We say an object is in free fall when gravity is the only thing acting on it. That rules out air resistance, the drag of the air on anything moving through it, which is why a leaf drifts down and a stone does not.

afterFigure.text: The picture shows a stone dropped from 80 m. Each second it adds another 10 m/s, and after 4 s it hits the ground at 40 m/s. That one steady gain is enough to predict the rest of the fall, starting with how fast the stone is going at any moment.

lead.text: A stone is dropped from the top of a tall cliff and falls freely.

reveal.text: The stone gains 10 m/s every second, so after 5 s it has gained 5 × 10 m/s.

lead.text: So far the numbers have only said how fast the stone goes. A throw also has a direction. The stone goes up for a while and then comes down, and signs are how we keep track of that. We choose one direction to count as positive, and in this lesson it is up. A height above the starting point is then positive, and so is a velocity that points upward.

Gravity pulls downward, so a stone dropped from rest soon moves downward, and its velocity is negative. After one second it is −10 m/s. Its acceleration is negative too, −10 m/s². The minus sign does not say the stone is slowing down. It says which way the velocity is changing, and here it is changing towards down. With u = 0 and a = −10, the rule from the last lesson gives v = 0 + (−10) × 4 = −40 m/s after 4 s.

afterFigure.text: The graph shows both cases that we meet in this lesson. For the dropped stone the velocity line slopes steadily downward from zero. For a stone thrown upward it starts above zero, falls through zero and carries on below. The slope of a velocity graph is the acceleration, so the two lines have the same slope because the two stones have the same acceleration.

lead.text: A ball is released from rest. Upward is positive.

reveal.text: You used v = u + at with a = −10. A negative velocity means the ball moves downward.

steps.headline: How far the stone has fallen

lead.text: Velocity tells us how fast. The next thing to predict is where the stone is. From the last lesson, the distance covered while speeding up at a steady rate is the average velocity times the time. A stone dropped from rest is going 10t m/s after t seconds, so over those t seconds its average velocity is half of that, 5t m/s. Multiplying by the time gives a distance fallen of 5t × t = 5t². In symbols that is ½gt², which is ½ × 10 × t².

After 1 s the stone has fallen 5 m. After 4 s it has fallen 5 × 4² = 80 m, sixteen times as far in a time only four times as long. Time is squared, so a fall that lasts twice as long covers four times the distance. In the picture a stone dropped from 80 m reaches the ground at exactly 4 s.

afterFigure.text: A distance fallen is not yet a height. With up as positive, the fall is a displacement of −½gt², and the height is where the stone started plus that displacement: height = starting height − ½gt². A stone dropped from 80 m is 5 m lower after 1 s, so it is at 75 m.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 80 m. How high is it after 3 s?

workedSteps.text: The ball moves down, so its displacement is negative.
Add the displacement to the starting height.

steps.headline: A ball is dropped from 45 m. How high is it after 2 s?

workedSteps.text: The distance fallen in 2 s is ½gt².
Take that fall off the starting height of 45 m.

lead.text: Now throw the stone straight up at 20 m/s. Gravity does not wait for the stone to start falling. It pulls down from the instant the stone leaves your hand, so the upward velocity shrinks by 10 m/s every second. It is 10 m/s after one second and zero after two. For an instant the stone is not moving at all, and that instant is the top of the throw. Afterwards its velocity is negative because it is heading down, and 2 s after the top it is back at your hand, moving at −20 m/s.

Look at what stays the same. The velocity goes from positive through zero to negative, but the acceleration is −10 m/s² all the way: on the way up, at the top and on the way down. A velocity of zero does not mean an acceleration of zero. At the top the velocity is changing as fast as at any other moment, and it is simply passing through zero on its way from up to down.

afterFigure.text: The height of a throw follows the same rule as before with the starting velocity u added in: displacement = ut − ½gt². For this stone at 2 s that is 20 × 2 − 5 × 2² = 20 m, so the top of the throw is 20 m above your hand. At 4 s it is 20 × 4 − 5 × 4² = 0, back where it started.

lead.text: Throw a ball straight up. It slows, stops for an instant at the top, then drops back.

reveal.text: The velocity is zero at the top but the acceleration is not. Gravity gave −10 on the way up and gives −10 now.

steps.headline: Does a heavy stone fall faster

lead.text: One question is left from the start of the lesson, whether a heavy stone falls faster than a light one. It seems obvious that it does, and a hammer and a feather dropped together seem to prove it. The picture is misleading because of the air. The feather catches the air and the hammer hardly does. In free fall nothing but gravity is acting, so there is no such difference to blame.

A heavy stone has more mass, the amount of matter in it, measured in kilograms. The acceleration we have used all lesson never mentioned mass, and that is the answer. Gravity does pull harder on a stone of larger mass, but the larger stone also has more matter to get moving. The two effects cancel exactly, so a 2 kg ball and an 8 kg ball let go together stay level all the way down.

afterFigure.text: In 1971 an astronaut on the Moon, where there is no air, dropped a hammer and a feather together. They reached the ground at the same moment.

lead.text: Two balls of different mass leave the same height at the same moment. Air resistance is ignored.

reveal.text: Mass cancels: a heavier ball is pulled harder but also has more to move. Free fall is the same for both.

lesson.orientation: Apply constant downward acceleration to free fall and an upward throw.
lesson.nextAction: Try the next idea, then return for a fresh problem after a delay.

blocks.text: Hold a stone out over the edge of a high bridge and let go. For the first instant it hardly seems to move. A moment later it is dropping quickly, and by the time it reaches the river you can barely follow it. Throw the same stone straight up and it does something just as odd. It climbs, slows, hangs for a moment at the top and then comes back down.

The last lesson ended with a way to predict where a cart will be when it speeds up at a steady rate. Gravity turns out to be a steady rate too, so the same sums describe the stone on its way down, on its way up and in the instant between.

We follow one stone. We drop it and work out how fast it goes and how far it falls, then throw it upward and watch what gravity does at the top. The last stop is an old argument, whether a heavy stone falls faster than a light one.

intro.promise: By the end you'll predict the velocity and height of a falling or thrown ball, and say what gravity does at the top.

recap.keyIdea: Free fall has one constant acceleration, 10 m/s² downward, whether the object rises, falls or sits at the top. Mass does not change it.

blocks.text: You worked out that a stone is going 50 m/s after falling for 5 s, and that a ball dropped from 45 m is 25 m up after 2 s. You also saw that a ball thrown upward has an acceleration of −10 m/s² at its highest point, where its velocity is zero.

recap.nextHook: Gravity is seldom the only pull on an object. Next we add up several pushes and pulls and see what they do together.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from rest. Take upward as positive and g = 10 m/s², with no air resistance. Find its velocity after 2 s, in m/s.
hints: Gravity points opposite to the positive direction.
Use negative acceleration in v = u + at.
Calculate 0 − 10 × 2.
questions.onCorrect: −20 m/s. The ball gains 10 m/s of downward velocity each second, and downward is negative here.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the ball moves down. With upward positive, its velocity is negative.
That is the velocity after one second only. The ball keeps gaining speed for 2 s.

questions.prompt: A ball is released from height 45 m. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, what is its height after 2 s, in metres?
hints: Find the downward displacement from rest.
Subtract ½gt² from the starting height.
Calculate 45 − 0.5 × 10 × 4.
questions.onCorrect: 25 m. Height is the start plus the signed displacement, and falling gives a negative displacement.

misconceptions.feedback: That adds the fall to the starting height. The ball goes down, so subtract it.
That uses the distance for 1 s of falling. The ball falls for 2 s.

questions.prompt: At the highest point of a vertical throw, find the acceleration in m/s². Take upward positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance.
hints: Separate zero velocity from zero acceleration.
Gravity continues acting throughout the flight.
Use the downward value of g with upward positive.

answerAuthority.workedAnswer: Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.

questions.onCorrect: −10 m/s². Velocity is zero at the top for an instant, but gravity keeps pulling down.

misconceptions.feedback: The velocity is zero there, not the acceleration. Gravity still acts at the top.
The size is right, but the pull is downward. With upward positive it needs a minus sign.

questions.prompt: Two objects of different mass are released together from the same height in the same gravitational field. Ignore air resistance. Which lands first?
hints: Check whether mass appears in the free-fall position equation.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.

questions.onCorrect: They land together. Without air resistance, free-fall acceleration does not depend on mass.

misconceptions.feedback: A bigger weight is balanced by a bigger mass to move. Without air resistance, the two cancel.
Mass does not appear in the free-fall equations. Both objects move the same way.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 30 m/s. With g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance, find its displacement after 2 s in metres.
hints: Combine the initial upward motion with the downward acceleration.
Use ut − ½gt².
Calculate 60 − 20.
questions.onCorrect: 40 m. Distance from the initial velocity, minus the amount gravity takes back.

misconceptions.feedback: That ignores gravity. The ball slows as it rises, so it goes less far than that.
That subtracts the wrong way round. Gravity takes distance off, it does not add.

questions.prompt: While a freely thrown ball is moving upward, which direction does its acceleration point? Ignore air resistance.
hints: The direction of motion does not determine the direction of gravitational acceleration.

answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.

choices.label: Upward, because the ball is rising
It has no acceleration until it falls

questions.onCorrect: Downward, towards Earth. Gravity gives the same downward acceleration on the way up, at the top and on the way down.

misconceptions.feedback: The direction of motion does not set the direction of acceleration. A rising ball is slowing.
Gravity acts the moment the ball leaves the hand, not when it starts to fall.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest and falls freely. How fast is it going after 5 s, in m/s? Use g = 10 m/s².
hints: How much speed does it gain in one second?
The gain is the same every second.
Multiply the gain per second by 5.
questions.onCorrect: 50 m/s. The stone gains 10 m/s every second, so five seconds of falling add 50 m/s.

misconceptions.feedback: That is the gain in one second. The stone keeps gaining for all 5.
That adds the time to the gain. Multiply them.

questions.prompt: A stone is dropped from rest. Take upward as positive, g = 10 m/s² and no air resistance. What is its velocity after 3 s, in m/s?
hints: With upward positive, which sign does gravity's acceleration have?
Use v = u + at, with u = 0.
Multiply the acceleration by 3 s.
questions.onCorrect: −30 m/s. Acceleration −10 m/s² for 3 s. The minus sign says the stone is moving down.

misconceptions.feedback: The size is right, but the stone moves down. With upward positive, that is a negative velocity.
That is the velocity after one second only. Multiply by the full 3 s.

questions.prompt: Why is the displacement of a falling ball negative here?
hints: Read each choice against the situation before you answer.

acceptedIdeas: It points downward, and upward is positive.
answerAuthority.exampleAnswer: It points downward, and upward is positive.

choices.label: It points downward, and upward is positive.
The ball loses mass as it falls.
Gravity is always a negative number.

questions.onCorrect: Signs follow the direction chosen as positive. A downward move is negative when up is positive.

misconceptions.feedback: Mass does not change in a fall. The sign comes from the direction chosen as positive.
Gravity is negative only because downward was chosen as the negative direction.

questions.prompt: A ball is thrown upward at 25 m/s. Take g = 10 m/s² and ignore air resistance. What is its velocity after 2 s, in m/s? Upward is positive.
hints: Gravity takes 10 m/s off the upward velocity every second.
How much does it take off in 2 s?
Take that away from the starting velocity.
questions.onCorrect: +5 m/s. The ball is still rising, but 20 m/s slower than it started.

misconceptions.feedback: The ball is still moving upward after 2 s, because it started fast enough. Check the sign.
That adds the velocity gravity takes away. Gravity acts downward, so it slows the ball.

citations.claim: A freely falling stone gains about 10 m/s of velocity every second, an acceleration g of 9.8 m/s² (10 m/s² in this course), and free fall means gravity is the only thing acting.
A stone dropped from rest is going 10 × 5 = 50 m/s after 5 s.
With up as positive, a falling object has negative velocity and an acceleration of −10 m/s², and v = u + at gives −40 m/s after 4 s from rest.
A ball released from rest has v = 0 + (−10) × 2 = −20 m/s after 2 s, upward positive.
From rest the distance fallen is ½gt², so 5 m after 1 s and 80 m after 4 s, and the height is the starting height minus that distance.
A ball dropped from 80 m has fallen ½ × 10 × 3² = 45 m after 3 s, so it is at 35 m.
A ball dropped from 45 m has fallen 20 m after 2 s, so it is at 25 m.
A stone thrown up at 20 m/s has velocity 0 after 2 s and rises 20 × 2 − ½ × 10 × 2² = 20 m; its acceleration stays −10 m/s² throughout.
At the top of a throw the velocity is zero but the acceleration is still −10 m/s².
Without air resistance, objects of different mass fall with the same acceleration, because the larger pull on a larger mass is cancelled by the larger mass to accelerate.
Two balls of different mass released together from the same height land together when air resistance is ignored.
Gravity still gives acceleration −10 m/s² at the top; only the instantaneous velocity is zero.
The same initial velocity and gravitational acceleration give the same motion in this model.
Displacement = 30 × 2 − ½ × 10 × 2² = 40 m upward.
The gravitational acceleration points downward throughout the flight, including while velocity points upward.
It points downward, and upward is positive.
v = 25 − 10 × 2 = +5 m/s, still rising.
With downward positive, v = 0 + 10 × 3 = 30 m/s.
